title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
text: Goal: recreate four interactive target plots with Plotly in Python. Part 2 (R) has four different plots, so together the two notebooks introduce eight kinds of Plotly charts. There is also one optional bonus plot at the end of this notebook.

title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
text:
How this works

Open each target plot in your web browser by double clicking the file in target-plots/. Hover over the data, drag to zoom, double click to reset, and click legend entries. Plotly gives you all of this automatically.
Read the checklist under each plot, then write your code in the empty cell. The hints give you a starting line of code.
Run the cell and compare your plot with the target. Adjust until they look the same.
When you are done, render this notebook with Quarto (see Submission at the bottom).

title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
text:
How close is close enough?
Get as close to the target as you can: same chart type, same data, same colors, same title and axis labels. Small differences in appearance are fine and will not lose points. Missing parts of the plot, wrong data, or unlabeled axes will.

text:
Tips for every plot

The setup cell gives you ORIGIN_COLORS, ORIGIN_ORDER, and LABELS. Pass them to every plot like this so your colors, legend order, and axis labels match the targets:
color_discrete_map=ORIGIN_COLORS,
category_orders={"origin": ORIGIN_ORDER},
labels=LABELS,
template="plotly_white",
Add a title with title="...". Copy the title text from the target.
Each plot is one call to a Plotly Express function (px.scatter, px.violin, px.line). The checklist tells you which arguments to add.

section: Plot 1: Scatter plot with marginal plots
text:
Plot 1: Scatter plot with marginal plots

Target: target-plots/plot-1_python_scatter-marginals.html
You will practice: a basic scatter plot, color groups, hover names, marginal plots

What to reproduce

weight on the x axis, mpg on the y axis, one color per origin
A histogram of weight above the scatter plot and box plots of mpg on the right
Hovering over a point shows the car name in bold

Hints

Start with fig1 = px.scatter(cars, x="weight", y="mpg", color="origin"), then add the standard arguments from the tips above
Marginal plots are one argument each: marginal_x="histogram", marginal_y="box"
The bold car name in the hover comes from hover_name="name"
Show the figure with fig1.show()
Docs: Scatter plots, Marginal plots

title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
text:
Plot 2: Animated bubble chart

Target: target-plots/plot-2_python_animated-scatter.html
You will practice: bubble sizes, animation with a play button and slider

What to reproduce

horsepower on the x axis, mpg on the y axis, colored by origin
Bubble size set by displacement
One animation frame per model_year, with a play button and slider
Axes stay fixed while it plays: x from 40 to 240, y from 5 to 50

Hints

New arguments for px.scatter(): size="displacement", animation_frame="model_year"
Fix the axes with range_x=[40, 240] and range_y=[5, 50]. Try leaving them out and pressing play to see why they matter
Keep hover_name="name" from Plot 1
Docs: Animations

title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
section: Plot 4: Line chart with a range slider
text:
Plot 4: Line chart with a range slider

Target: target-plots/plot-4_python_line-rangeslider.html
You will practice: summarizing data first, line charts, range sliders

What to reproduce

The average mpg for each model year and origin, one line per origin with markers
A range slider under the x axis. Drag its ends to zoom in on a range of years

Hints

First compute the averages. This line is given to you:
yearly = cars.groupby(["model_year", "origin"], as_index=False)["mpg"].mean()
Then plot the new yearly data frame: fig4 = px.line(yearly, x="model_year", y="mpg", color="origin", markers=True, ...)
Add the slider after creating the figure: fig4.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
Docs: Line charts, Range slider

title: Plotly Assignment, Part 1: Python
section: Bonus A: dropdown menu with graph objects
text:
Bonus A: dropdown menu with graph objects
Optional, worth 1 bonus point. Skip it if you like; leave the cell empty or delete it.

Target: target-plots/bonus-A_python_dropdown-menu.html
You will practice: plotly.graph_objects, building traces yourself, dropdown menus

What to reproduce

The same yearly averages as Plot 4, but for mpg, horsepower, and weight
Built with plotly.graph_objects, not Plotly Express: one go.Scatter trace per origin
A dropdown menu at the top right that switches the lines between the three variables and updates the y axis title
Hovering on a year shows all three origins in one box

Hints

This one is a step up, and it is optional. Plotly Express builds traces for you; here you build them yourself.
Averages: cars.groupby(["model_year", "origin"], as_index=False)[["mpg", "horsepower", "weight"]].mean()
Build the figure: import plotly.graph_objects as go, figA = go.Figure(), then loop over ORIGIN_ORDER and call figA.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=..., y=..., name=origin, mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color=ORIGIN_COLORS[origin])))
A dropdown is a list of buttons in figA.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(buttons=[...])]). Each button replaces the y data of all three traces (in order) and changes the axis title:
dict(label="Horsepower", method="update",
     args=[{"y": [usa_values, europe_values, japan_values]},
           {"yaxis.title.text": "Horsepower"}])
Combined hover: hovermode="x unified" in update_layout
Docs: Graph objects, Dropdown menus

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Streamlit first · Dash as optional supplemental material
Lecture 1 of 2: The next packet introduces Shiny in R.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Where does a visualization run?


Static graphic: rendered once; export a PNG, SVG, or PDF (Matplotlib, Seaborn, ggplot2).
Client-side interactive graphic: browser handles zoom, hover, and selection (Plotly.js, Vega-Lite).
Server-backed data app: browser controls trigger Python/R calculations, queries, or models (Streamlit, Dash, Shiny).
These categories overlap: a Streamlit app can display an interactive Plotly chart.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
The internet in one picture


A browser (client) requests a page from a web server.
The server returns HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and possibly data.
The browser displays the page; later interactions may or may not require another server request.
Historical diagram note: Java applets are obsolete; modern web apps generally use JavaScript and web APIs.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Frontend vs. backend


Frontend (browser): what users see and click; HTML/CSS/JavaScript.
Backend (server): Python/R code that loads data, runs models, queries databases, and returns results.
A server can be your own laptop during development—not necessarily a cloud machine.
Streamlit hides much of the web plumbing, but a server process still runs Python.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: Compare: Plotly HTML vs. a Streamlit app
text:
Compare: Plotly HTML vs. a Streamlit app








Question
Standalone Plotly HTML
Streamlit app




Where does interaction happen?
Mostly in browser
Browser and Python server


Hover, zoom, toggle traces?
Yes
Yes (via embedded Plotly chart)


Re-run Python after a widget changes?
No
Yes


Query a database or score a model on demand?
Not without another service
Yes, from Python


Share as a static file?
Often yes
Requires running app server



Key idea: A Plotly chart can be interactive without a Python backend. A Streamlit app can recompute its data and charts when inputs change.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
A concrete example: exploring sales
Client-side-only: A user hovers over a precomputed sales chart or hides a product series.
Server-backed: A user chooses a region → Python filters millions of records (or queries a database) → computes a new forecast → sends updated results to the browser.

A backend unlocks fresh data, expensive computation, authentication, and coordinated controls.
Tradeoff: hosting, latency, cost, and security become important.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
How a server-backed visualization works
Browser                     Python server
[Choose a region] --------> [Read selection]
                            [Filter / query data]
                            [Compute / fit model]
[Updated chart] <---------- [Return results]

The UI collects inputs and presents outputs.
The server does work that cannot be packaged as a self-contained HTML chart.
A browser is still responsible for rendering the final visualization.

Both ecosystems can embed Plotly and other interactive chart libraries.
BI platforms (Power BI, Tableau) emphasize managed reporting; frameworks emphasize custom behavior and computation.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: Hosting: where does the backend live?
text:
Hosting: where does the backend live?

Local: run on your laptop for development; browser connects to localhost.
Hosted: deploy to an appropriate cloud/app platform so others can open a URL.
Hosting must keep the Python/R process running and provide required packages and data access.
Public hosting is not automatically private: avoid committing passwords, tokens, or sensitive datasets.
Containerization (e.g., Docker) can help package dependencies, but is not needed for our first app.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: Agentic coding: another way to build data apps
text:
Agentic coding: another way to build data apps

AI coding assistants can help plan, generate, run, debug, and revise application code.
A prompt might be: “Build a Streamlit dashboard that filters a CSV and plots sales by month.”
This can speed up prototyping and let analysts explore unfamiliar frameworks.
It does not remove the need to understand data, logic, and deployment.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Working responsibly with AI-generated applications

Start with a clear specification: dataset, inputs, expected outputs, and audience.
Run locally; inspect the code; verify chart values against known examples.
Check dependencies, secrets, data permissions, and error handling.
Ask the assistant to explain each component and simplify unfamiliar code.
Takeaway: AI is a collaborator, not a substitute for validation. We may revisit full app-building workflows later in the course.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
What is Streamlit?

Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for making interactive data applications.
Write ordinary Python scripts with functions such as st.title(), st.slider(), and st.plotly_chart().
Streamlit supplies the browser interface and runs your Python code on a server.
Great for prototypes, course projects, exploratory dashboards, and model demos.

Mental model: write a Python script that describes the page.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Install and launch
From a terminal in your project directory:
python -m pip install streamlit pandas plotly
Create a file called app.py. Run:
streamlit run app.py

Open the local URL printed in the terminal (typically http://localhost:8501).
Save edits to app.py; Streamlit can rerun the app.
Important: Run a Streamlit app from a terminal—not as a normal Jupyter code cell.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: First app: text and a table
text:
First app: text and a table
Save this as app.py:
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

st.title("My first data app")
st.write("Explore a tiny dataset with Python.")

data = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"],
                     "sales": [120, 150, 135]})
st.dataframe(data)

st.title() creates a heading.
st.write() displays text or many Python objects.
st.dataframe() provides a scrollable, interactive table.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Add a widget: the slider
import streamlit as st

st.title("Interactive input")
minimum_sales = st.slider("Minimum sales", 0, 200, 100)
st.write("Selected threshold:", minimum_sales)

st.slider() returns the user’s chosen value.
Changing a widget typically reruns the Python script from top to bottom.
The widget’s current value is available on each rerun.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
section: Connect an input to a visualization
text:
Connect an input to a visualization
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import streamlit as st

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"],
    "sales": [120, 150, 135, 180],
})
threshold = st.slider("Minimum sales", 0, 200, 100)
filtered = sales[sales["sales"] >= threshold]

fig = px.bar(filtered, x="month", y="sales", title="Monthly sales")
st.plotly_chart(fig, use_container_width=True)
Notice: Python filters the data; Plotly handles chart interactions in the browser.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
A complete small dashboard
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import streamlit as st

st.title("Sales explorer")
df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "East", "West", "West"],
                   "month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Jan", "Feb"],
                   "sales": [120, 160, 90, 140]})
region = st.selectbox("Region", sorted(df["region"].unique()))
view = df[df["region"] == region]
st.metric("Total sales", f"${view['sales'].sum():,.0f}")
st.plotly_chart(px.bar(view, x="month", y="sales"),
                use_container_width=True)
st.dataframe(view)

One selection drives a metric, chart, and table.
This is a server-backed dashboard, even though its dataset is small.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Layout: organize a dashboard
import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(page_title="Explorer", layout="wide")
st.title("Explorer")

with st.sidebar:
    year = st.selectbox("Year", [2024, 2025, 2026])

left, right = st.columns(2)
with left:
    st.metric("Selected year", year)
with right:
    st.info("Place a chart or table here.")

Sidebar: controls that affect the whole page.
Columns: place related outputs side by side.
st.set_page_config() belongs near the beginning of the script.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Loading your own data
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

uploaded = st.file_uploader("Choose a CSV", type="csv")
if uploaded is not None:
    df = pd.read_csv(uploaded)
    st.write("Rows:", len(df))
    st.dataframe(df.head())
else:
    st.info("Upload a CSV to begin.")

Files are supplied by the user through the browser.
Validate file types, column names, and missing values before plotting.
Do not assume that a shared app’s uploads are appropriate for sensitive data.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Streamlit’s rerun model

The script normally runs top to bottom when a user changes a widget.
Widget values are re-created from the current browser session.
This makes small apps simple, but repeated data loading can be slow.
Ask: Which operations should happen on every interaction?

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Build a useful app: checklist

Identify the question the dashboard should answer.
Load and validate the dataset.
Add one meaningful control (region, year, category).
Compute a filtered view in Python.
Display a chart and a summary metric.
Test extreme selections and empty results.
Share the app only after checking its data and access permissions.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Knowledge check

If you export a Plotly figure to HTML, does it require a running Python server to hover and zoom?
What changes when a Streamlit slider is moved?
Why might a server-backed dashboard be more powerful than a static HTML report?
What additional responsibility appears when an app is deployed publicly?

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Cache expensive work
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_data
def load_data(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path)

df = load_data("sales.csv")
st.dataframe(df.head())

st.cache_data is for reusable data results; cache entries can be shared across sessions.
Use st.cache_resource for reusable resources such as model objects or connections.
Choose caching carefully when data changes or contains user-specific information.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Remember values across reruns
import streamlit as st

if "clicks" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.clicks = 0

if st.button("Count a click"):
    st.session_state.clicks += 1

st.write("Clicks in this session:", st.session_state.clicks)

st.session_state retains values for a user session across reruns.
Forms, tabs, multipage navigation, and callbacks offer additional control.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Deployment and reproducibility

Keep app.py and a dependency file (such as requirements.txt) together.
Test locally from a clean environment before publishing.
Use a Streamlit-compatible hosting service or your own server/container.
Store secrets using platform-supported secret management—not in Git.
Check server logs, package versions, data access, and user permissions.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Where Dash fits

Dash is a Python framework from Plotly for interactive web applications.
Uses explicit layout components and callbacks to connect inputs to outputs.
Often useful when you want more precise control over how UI events update specific outputs.
Streamlit usually offers a shorter path to a first analytical dashboard.
Both require a running Python app server for server-side functionality.

title: Server-Side Visualization Tools in Python
text:
Minimal Dash example
Install: python -m pip install dash plotly
from dash import Dash, dcc, html, Input, Output
import plotly.express as px

app = Dash(__name__)
app.layout = html.Div([
    dcc.Slider(1, 5, 1, id="minimum"),
    dcc.Graph(id="chart"),
])

@app.callback(Output("chart", "figure"), Input("minimum", "value"))
def update_chart(minimum):
    df = px.data.iris()
    return px.scatter(df[df.sepal_length >= minimum],
                      x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length",
                      color="species")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)
Run: python app.py. The callback connects slider changes to the figure.
